concept_mcqs.stem:
You inherit this draft charter excerpt:
```text
Project: Returns Portal Improvement
Problem statement: Customers sometimes face issues returning items.
Objectives: Make returns easier.
Scope: TBD after we talk to users.
Assumptions: None documented.
Constraints: Must reuse existing payment gateway contract (no new providers in FY).
Stakeholders: CX Lead, Warehouse Ops Manager, Finance Controller.
```
Your elicitation start date is next week. To reduce rework and scope creep downstream, what is the most effective next step before you begin technique-specific sessions?
options: Send a company-wide survey to collect all potential improvements first, then scope later.
Start interviews with end users only and let the scope emerge over time.
Schedule a cross-functional scoping workshop to draft explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists tied to objectives.
Proceed directly to observation so “the work speaks for itself,” deferring scope until after shadowing.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With a vague problem statement and no scope boundaries, starting elicitation will surface solution ideas that collide with hidden constraints. A short, cross-functional scoping workshop to write explicit in-scope/out-of-scope items anchored to objectives reduces churn and frames subsequent interviews, observations, and surveys.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is tempting because interviews feel foundational, but without boundaries they create divergent inputs and rework. C sounds efficient but will explode idea volume without a frame, worsening scope ambiguity. D overvalues observation; while useful, it still needs scope anchors to decide what to watch and why.

concept_mcqs.stem:
During a sponsor interview, you capture this exchange:
```text
BA: What impact are the current return steps having on our Q4 targets?
Sponsor: We just need a one-click refund button. That will fix it.
BA: If we had that, what changes would you expect to see?
Sponsor: Fewer calls. Faster close.
```
You need to prevent solution bias and still progress. What should you do next in the interview?
options: Refocus on outcomes and metrics by probing measurable impacts (e.g., call handle time, first contact resolution) and conditions where they occur.
Switch to closed yes/no questions to stay on schedule and avoid debate.
State the button idea is out of scope per charter and move on to another topic.
Accept the solution and mark a high-priority requirement to maintain executive alignment.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Reframing to outcomes and measurable impacts keeps the sponsor engaged while de-biasing the discussion. It anchors later elicitation (across techniques) on the problem effects instead of a preselected solution.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B may be necessary later if scope truly conflicts, but early hard rejection harms rapport and may be premature. C preserves relationship but bakes in solution bias that distorts the rest of elicitation. D speeds the meeting but further reduces learning and invites confirmation bias.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Here is a draft survey question set meant to prioritise pain points:
```text
Q1. How satisfied are you with the speed and accuracy of the returns portal?
    Scale: Very dissatisfied / Dissatisfied / Neutral / Satisfied / Very satisfied
Q2. What would you change to improve it? (optional)
```
Your goal is to produce data that indicates which aspect to fix first without conflating issues. What is the best change?
options: Reduce the sample to known power users so the responses come from experts who can articulate trade-offs.
Make the free-text Q2 mandatory so you always know the specific issue per respondent.
Add an NPS question to benchmark overall sentiment; leave Q1 as is for comparability.
Split Q1 into two separate items (speed, accuracy) and use a task-frequency or time-based scale for speed rather than general satisfaction.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The current Q1 is double-barrelled and uses a vague satisfaction scale. Separating speed and accuracy and measuring speed with a frequency/time proxy yields actionable, non-conflated signals for prioritisation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B adds a metric but not the diagnostic separation needed. C increases response burden and noise, and mandated text still won’t deconfound speed vs accuracy. D narrows to a biased subpopulation and undermines generalisability.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your observation log shows this pattern:
```text
2026-02-12 10:05  Agent A processes refund in 4 steps when supervisor at desk
2026-02-12 14:40  Agent A uses 7-step workaround when supervisor away
2026-02-13 09:15  Agent B states “we always follow SOP” but uses keyboard macro unseen in SOP when supervisor passes by
```
To reduce bias in the data you collect next week, what change to your elicitation plan is most appropriate?
options: Ask agents to self-record their screens only when they solve unusual cases to reduce observer effects.
Add unobtrusive shadowing sessions across shifts without supervisor presence, with prior consent and clear purpose, to observe natural behaviour.
Replace observation with a larger survey so participants feel anonymous.
Invite supervisors into a workshop to clarify the SOP so everyone aligns on the official process.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The pattern suggests observer or authority-proximity effects. Scheduling consented, low-intrusion shadowing across contexts without supervisor presence reduces this bias and triangulates with prior logs.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B anonymity helps honesty but loses behavioural evidence. C may clarify rules but not actual practice under conditions that trigger workarounds. D selectively samples unusual cases and increases self-selection and novelty bias.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your charter currently says:
```text
Scope (In): Returns portal UI changes, warehouse disposition codes
Scope (Out): Payment provider integrations and any refund automation touching payment rails
Constraints: Existing gateway contract through FY
```
In a workshop, participants propose "automated refunds for low-value items". What should you do next to preserve governance and momentum?
options: Log it as a risk so it remains visible while you continue as planned.
Escalate the idea through the charter’s change authority for impact assessment and, if approved, update scope before carrying it into the backlog.
Drop the idea from notes to avoid distracting the group from in-scope work.
Include it as a stretch goal in the charter to keep teams motivated without formal change.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The proposal directly conflicts with explicit out-of-scope items and a contract constraint. Routing via change control ensures traceability and prevents illegitimate scope expansion.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B mislabels a scope addition as a risk, weakening control. C creates a backdoor scope creep without authority. D hides stakeholder input and erodes trust.

You drafted this 90-minute workshop agenda for mixed seniority participants:
```text
0–15  Sponsor context (slides)
15–25 Clarifying Q&A (plenary)
25–55 Open brainstorming (plenary)
55–80 Group discussion and clustering (plenary)
80–90 Next steps
```
Senior leaders tend to speak first and set direction. What is the single most effective facilitation change to reduce anchoring and groupthink while preserving the 90-minute slot?
options: Replace the open brainstorm with two silent brainwriting rounds followed by clustering before any plenary sharing.
Extend the sponsor’s context to 30 minutes so everyone agrees on goals first.
Replace the workshop with an anonymous survey to eliminate social pressure entirely.
Use cold-calling during the plenary brainstorm to ensure junior voices are heard.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Silent brainwriting ensures idea generation before exposure to dominant voices, reducing anchoring and groupthink while keeping the timebox.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B increases anchoring. C can help distribution but ideas are still shaped by early speakers. D throws away collaborative synthesis and doesn’t resolve ambiguity inherent in brainstorming.

```csv
Sponsor,1 person,Friday 09:00–09:30 only
```

options: Cancel observation and do a single joint workshop next Monday with whoever can join to accelerate alignment.

Use the sponsor’s Friday slot first to get direction, then interview Ops leads Monday, and observe agents later via recordings.
Send a survey to all parties to capture inputs quickly, then observe agents if time permits.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Observing real work first yields grounded questions for Ops leads. You can then brief the sponsor with evidence-backed insights, making the short slot effective. This ordering respects availability and data quality.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B risks solution bias from the sponsor shaping questions. C trades depth and validity for speed. D compresses diverse roles into a rushed session that invites dominance and shallow outputs.

```text
Observation: 2 hours on Site A returns desk, Tuesday morning
Workshops: Cross-functional group (Site A personnel)
```

Given the problem spans three sites and all shifts, what is the most critical fix to reduce sampling bias without exploding scope?
options: Stratify the sample to include reps across sites and shifts (e.g., add Site B/C and at least one night shift) and proportionally extend observation.
Rely on the cross-functional workshop to surface cross-site issues rather than expanding interviews.
Add a broad customer survey instead of changing the staff sample.
Double interview count at Site A to 16 to improve confidence.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The plan is site- and shift-biased. Stratified sampling across sites/shifts plus proportional observation yields more representative data with controlled expansion.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B increases quantity without fixing bias. C surveys a different population and does not correct staff operational bias. D workshops risk hearsay and dominance, not representative operational evidence.

Legal sends this note before interviews and observation:
```text
Subject: Recording and PII
If you plan to record sessions, ensure explicit consent is captured. Retain recordings max 30 days. Mask PII where practicable.
```
What change should you make to your plan to remain compliant while preserving data quality?
options: Proceed with recording as planned but add a blanket NDA for all participants.
Skip recording entirely and rely on handwritten notes to avoid privacy issues.
Integrate a recorded-consent script and tracking, document retention/deletion dates, and define a masking process for any PII captured.
Record only audio, not screens, so PII won’t be captured.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Explicit consent with tracked retention and a masking workflow meets legal guidance while keeping high-fidelity data. The plan change is concrete and auditable.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B throws away fidelity and may still capture PII in notes. C NDAs don’t replace consent and retention controls. D audio alone can still include PII and removes critical behavioural context.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Two competing draft problem statements appear in the charter:
```text
Version 1: We must implement automated refunds so customers don’t call support.
Version 2: High call volume related to returns increases handling costs and delays refunds, risking SLA breaches in Q4.
```
Which rewrite will best guide elicitation by focusing on the underlying problem and measurable impacts without prescribing a solution?
options: Returns are too slow; the team must speed them up as quickly as possible to hit targets.
Customers dislike the portal, so we should redesign it to be more user friendly and modern.
Employees are using too many workarounds, so we should enforce the SOP more strictly.
High return-related call volume increases handling cost by 18% and delays refunds beyond 48 hours for 22% of cases; we need to understand causes across portal, policy, and operations before Q4.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Option A names the effect and magnitude, sets measurable targets, and keeps solution space open, which steers elicitation toward causes across people, process, and technology.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is solution-prescriptive and vague. C states a desire without diagnostics or measures. D narrows prematurely to enforcement and assumes the SOP is correct, stifling discovery.

scenario_questions.scenario:
You receive a messy intake with fragments from three emails and a whiteboard photo after a hurried kickoff:
```text
Email 1 (Sponsor): "Need fewer return calls. Quick win pls."
Email 2 (Ops Lead): "Warehouse rework up 12%. Suspect wrong disposition codes from portal."
Email 3 (Finance): "Refunds breaching 48h SLA up from 5% to 22% in Q3. Gateway contract fixed till FY end."
Whiteboard photo transcription: IN: portal screens; OUT: payments? (unclear). Assumptions: agents follow SOP. Stakeholders: CX, Ops, Finance. TBD: Customers, Legal.
```
The current charter draft reflects this confusion. You must sharpen the problem definition and scope before elicitation starts.
scenario_questions.task: Write a crisp problem statement, a first-pass success metric set, and explicit scope boundaries (in-scope and out-of-scope) that reconcile the evidence. List at least four stakeholders to engage early and justify each choice based on the artefacts.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong answer articulates an outcome-focused, measurable problem such as: "Return-related contacts increased 28% and refunds breaching 48h rose to 22% in Q3, driving handling cost and SLA risk. Causes may span portal data capture, agent workflow, and policy; payment provider changes are constrained by the FY contract." Success metrics include reduced return-related call volume by a defined target, <5% refunds breaching 48h, and reduced warehouse rework. Scope in includes portal return flows, agent handoffs, and disposition code mapping; scope out includes new payment provider integrations while the contract stands. Stakeholders include Sponsor (decision rights), Ops Lead (process owner), Finance (SLA and cost), Warehouse (rework impact), Legal/Compliance (recording, PII), Customer Support Agents (frontline behaviour), and potentially a Customer Panel (external perspective). Justifications tie each stakeholder to specific lines in the artefacts (e.g., Finance’s SLA data, Ops’ rework claim).

rubric.criterion: Problem statement is outcome-focused, non-prescriptive, and reconciles conflicting fragments with appropriate qualifiers (e.g., constraints).
Success metrics are specific, measurable, and traceable to the stated problem (at least two, with directional targets).
Scope boundaries clearly list in-scope and out-of-scope items with rationale tied to evidence (e.g., payment provider constraint).
Stakeholder list includes at least four roles with clear justification linked to the artefacts’ concerns.

scenario_questions.scenario: Your organisation is distributed across three sites with mixed shifts. Time windows are constrained as in the earlier MCQ. Legal requires explicit recording consent and 30-day retention. Supervisors tend to influence agent behaviour when present. The sponsor can only spare 30 minutes on Friday morning during week 1.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a one-week elicitation plan that sequences interviews, observation, workshops, and surveys to maximise validity under these constraints. Specify who, what method, duration, consent/recording approach, and expected artefacts per session. Include two concrete bias/risks you will mitigate and how.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: An effective plan opens with contextual observation of end-user agents across at least two sites and shifts (no supervisors present; consent captured via a standard script; 30-day retention logged). Follow with targeted 30–45 minute Ops lead interviews informed by observed pain points. Schedule a 60–90 minute cross-functional workshop with silent brainwriting to synthesise findings and map causes to data points, ensuring legal/PII constraints are addressed. Use a short, split-question survey to validate specific hypotheses about speed vs accuracy for a broader audience. Close with a 30-minute sponsor brief on Friday presenting evidence-backed impacts and options. Artefacts include observation logs and timing data, interview notes, consent records, workshop outputs (clusters, prioritised themes), and survey results. Bias mitigations include stratified sampling across sites/shifts to reduce sampling bias and brainwriting to reduce anchoring; privacy risks mitigated by consent tracking and data deletion scheduling.

rubric.criterion: Clear, feasible sequence mapping each method to specific stakeholder groups with durations and outputs.
Consent and retention controls specified and workable within policy (script, tracking, deletion date).
At least two concrete biases/risks identified with method-specific mitigations tied to the scenario (e.g., supervisor effect, sampling bias).
Plan leverages early evidence to inform later sessions (e.g., observation informs interview guides; workshop synthesises).

scenario_questions.scenario:
After initial rounds, you have conflicting signals:
```text
Interviews (Agents): "Portal slow; we follow SOP."
Observation timing: Median refund path 2m 10s with supervisor away; 1m 20s when supervisor present (fewer validation steps used).
Warehouse rework: Up 12% after agents use code R-07 more often on busy mornings.
```
Ops insists the SOP is sufficient. Sponsor wants a quick UI fix.
scenario_questions.task: Formulate a testable hypothesis explaining the discrepancy and propose a targeted follow-up elicitation plan (two or more activities) to confirm or refute it. State what evidence would change your scope or priorities.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A good hypothesis is that time pressure and oversight change agent behaviour, leading to inconsistent code selection (R-07) and downstream rework; the UI may enable skipping validations under social pressure. Follow-ups could include unobtrusive time-sampled shadowing across peak/off-peak and with/without supervisor presence, plus think-aloud task-based interviews using realistic scenarios to see where validation steps are bypassed. Optionally extract system logs to correlate timestamps with code usage by shift. Evidence that code misuse correlates with peak times and reduced validation would shift scope toward workflow/policy and UI guardrails rather than pure performance tuning. If logs show consistent misuse regardless of conditions, UI affordances and training might dominate.

rubric.criterion: Hypothesis connects observed behaviour, context (supervisor/peak times), and downstream effects (rework) coherently.
Follow-up plan includes at least two appropriate techniques and explains how each will confirm/refute aspects of the hypothesis.
Decision criteria: states what specific evidence would shift scope or priority and in which direction.

scenario_questions.scenario: Participants for a cross-functional workshop include a vocal sponsor, two Ops leads, four agents, one Finance analyst, and Legal. Past sessions derailed into solutioning and status updates. Remote participants join from Sites B and C with variable bandwidth.
scenario_questions.task: Design a 75–90 minute workshop plan that keeps focus on the problem and evidence, minimises anchoring, and produces a prioritised set of causes to investigate. Specify activities, timings, roles, materials, and how you’ll handle remote participation and Legal’s constraints.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong plan includes a 5-minute framing with the chartered problem and metrics; 10 minutes of silent brainwriting on observed pain points and evidence; 15 minutes of small breakout clustering (mixed roles) with remote-friendly boards; 15 minutes dot-voting on cause clusters using criteria (impact, evidence strength); 20 minutes to map top clusters to data/evidence and identify knowledge gaps; 10 minutes to agree next steps. Roles: facilitator, timekeeper, scribe, sponsor as participant not presenter. Materials: virtual whiteboard with templates, consent reminder for any shared screenshots, and pre-read of observation snippets. Remote handling: short activities, explicit turn-taking, chat-based inputs as backup; record only with consent and assure retention limits. Legal is consulted on PII masking in shared artefacts.

rubric.criterion: Structure prioritises de-biasing (e.g., silent ideation) and problem focus before any solutioning.
Activities, timings, and roles are clear, feasible, and sum to 75–90 minutes.
Remote participation constraints addressed with specific tools/practices; Legal/PII considerations integrated.
Outputs lead to a prioritised, evidence-linked set of causes and explicit next steps.

practical_tasks.title: Produce a Project Charter for the Returns Improvement Initiative
practical_tasks.brief: Create a 2–4 page project charter that defines the problem, objectives, scope boundaries, stakeholders, assumptions, constraints, risks, and governance for the returns improvement effort. Use only information that could reasonably be known at this stage; make assumptions explicit and traceable.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A single PDF or DOCX named "Project_Charter_Returns_<YourName>.pdf|docx"
acceptance_criteria: Includes a problem statement that is measurable and non-prescriptive.
States 2–4 success metrics with current baseline (or how baseline will be obtained) and target direction.
Provides explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists with rationale tied to constraints (e.g., vendor contract).
Lists key stakeholders with role and a power–interest or RACI view.
Documents assumptions and constraints relevant to scope and scheduling.
Identifies 3–5 initial risks with owners and mitigation direction.
Specifies decision rights/change control for scope changes.
Contains version/date, author, and required approvals/sign-offs.
No placeholders like "TBD" without an accompanying plan to resolve; consistent terminology throughout.

rubric.criterion: Problem statement and success metrics are specific, measurable, and avoid prescribing solutions.
Scope boundaries (in/out) are clear, justified, and aligned to constraints; governance for changes is defined.
Stakeholder analysis (roles plus power–interest/RACI) is complete and actionable.
Assumptions, constraints, and initial risks are identified with owners/mitigations; document quality (clarity, consistency, versioning, approvals).

practical_tasks.title: Develop an Elicitation Plan for Week 1
practical_tasks.brief: Plan a one-week elicitation effort that selects and sequences interviews, workshops, observation, and surveys to investigate the returns problem. Address logistics, participants, consent/privacy, instruments, and risks.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A single PDF or DOCX named "Elicitation_Plan_Week1_<YourName>.pdf|docx" including schedule, participant list, and instrument outlines (interview guide, workshop agenda, survey draft).
acceptance_criteria: Includes a day-by-day schedule with session types, durations, participants, and expected artefacts.
Maps each elicitation method to specific objectives or hypotheses from the charter.
Provides an interview guide outline (topics and 6–10 non-leading questions) and a workshop agenda with de-biasing activities.
Provides a survey draft with deconfounded questions if a survey is used, or justification if not used.
Details consent/recording scripts, retention period, and PII masking approach per policy.
Addresses sampling strategy (e.g., sites/shifts) and logistical constraints.
Includes a risk/mitigation section for at least three risks (e.g., supervisor effect, sampling bias, low attendance).
Specifies how findings will be captured and stored (templates, repositories) and how traceability to objectives will be maintained.

rubric.criterion: Schedule and sequencing are feasible and aligned to objectives/hypotheses; participants and outputs are clear.
Quality of instruments: interview guide is non-leading; workshop agenda includes de-biasing; survey (if used) avoids double-barrel/leading scales.
Compliance and ethics: consent, retention, and PII masking are concrete and auditable.
Sampling strategy and risk mitigations address bias and logistical constraints; capture/traceability approach is defined.

You mapped the as-is order verification process and collected time data:

```csv
Step,Avg Wait (min),Avg Work (min),Defects per 100
Intake,12,4,1
Pre-Check,25,3,2
Approve,5,6,0.5
Fulfil,8,10,3
```
The business target is to cut total cycle time by 20% without adding headcount. Which to-be change is most likely to achieve the target by addressing the dominant root cause evident in the data?
options: Move data validation from Pre-Check into Intake with a form-level validator and required fields; demote Pre-Check to exception handling.
Add a second approver in parallel to reduce the Approve work time from 6 to 3 minutes.
Add WIP limits to Fulfil to keep no more than 2 orders being worked at once.
Automate label printing in Fulfil to shave 2 minutes of work time per order.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Wait time at Pre-Check (25 min) dwarfs other waits and work times, so front-loading validation to prevent queuing at Pre-Check removes the bottleneck. This attacks the largest contributor to total cycle time without adding people.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is tempting because it reduces a visible work time, but Approve’s work time (6) is small compared to the 25-minute Pre-Check wait. C improves Fulfil work time but addresses a smaller contributor. D may improve flow but does not remove the main root cause: the large queue created by late validation.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A 5 Whys on order delays produced this:

```text
Problem: Late shipments up 15%
Why1: Pick tickets queued ~2h
Why2: Queue because wave release at 10:00 only
Why3: Single daily batch configured
Why4: Batch due to fear of printer jams
Why5: No auto-retry policy defined
```
Which to-be change best addresses the root cause while maintaining control?
options: Add two additional pickers to drain the queue faster after 10:00.
Keep a single daily batch but add two more printers to avoid jams.
Allow ad-hoc manual waves when supervisors notice a queue.
Introduce hourly wave releases with an automatic print retry/backoff policy and alerting.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The root cause is the batching choice driven by printer-jam risk. Moving to frequent waves plus auto-retry and alerting addresses both flow and the original risk.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B treats the symptom (printer jams) but keeps the batch cadence that creates the queue. C adds capacity but leaves the batching constraint and creates cost. D relies on human detection and is inconsistent; it doesn’t fix the systemic batching root cause.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A refund flow is producing occasional double refunds. The BPMN fragment is below:

```xml
<process id="refund">
  <parallelGateway id="gw1"/>
  <sequenceFlow id="f1" sourceRef="gw1" targetRef="AutoRefund"/>
  <sequenceFlow id="f2" sourceRef="gw1" targetRef="ManualReview"/>
  <sequenceFlow id="to_pay" sourceRef="AutoRefund" targetRef="IssuePayment"/>
  <sequenceFlow id="to_pay2" sourceRef="ManualReview" targetRef="IssuePayment"/>
</process>
```
Which to-be correction prevents the defect while preserving intent that only one path should lead to payment?
options: Keep the model but guard IssuePayment with an idempotency check only.
Replace the parallel gateway with an exclusive gateway and define clear routing rules.
Add a non-interrupting boundary timer on AutoRefund to throttle duplicate payments.
Merge the two flows with another parallel gateway before IssuePayment to synchronize.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A parallel gateway forks both paths, enabling two payments. Using an exclusive gateway enforces a single route based on conditions, matching the business rule.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B treats a symptom (timing) but not the modeling error. C synchronizes two active paths and still risks double payment. D relies on implementation controls while leaving a logically incorrect process model.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A Visio as-is map duplicated a task in two lanes:

```text
- Rectangle: "Check Inventory" (Lane A)
- Rectangle: "Check Inventory" (Lane B)
- Subprocess: "Ship Order" (non-collapsed)

```
Later, analysts struggled to trace defects tied to "Check Inventory" because two shapes existed with no unique identity. What to-be modeling change most directly improves traceability and reuse?
options: Replace the duplicate rectangles with a single call activity (reusable subprocess) "Check Inventory" referenced from both lanes, with a unique ID.
Leave shapes as-is but add a footnote explaining they are the same logical step.
Convert both rectangles into separate subprocesses with the same name and different colors.
Keep both rectangles but add a bold border to the more important one.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A call activity (reusable subprocess) with a unique identifier provides a single traceable definition referenced from multiple contexts, fixing duplication and traceability gaps.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/Bold border adds emphasis, not identity. C creates two different definitions, worsening traceability. D relies on documentation rather than model semantics and is brittle.
